text.p: Black-coloured whisky and whisky flavoured with chilli peppers are being introduced to attract young British drinkers and boost sales in a declining market, said a spokesman for United Distillers, a subsidiary of Guinness Plc, on Thursday.

The black Whisky called Loch Dhu -- which is Gaelic for black lake -- achieves its colour through the use of charred oak casks. It is targeted at 25- to 35-year-olds who do not traditionally drink whisky.
United Distiller's consumer marketing director Andy Neal told Reuters "the black colour, smooth taste and contemporary image will encourage a more versatile usage".

The company is also testing a whisky blended with chilli peppers called Red Devil. It is currently on sale in some London bars and, if successful, may be launched nationally next year. While drinkers have grown used to vodka mixed with chilli, lemons and even blackcurrants, it is believed to be the first whisky of its kind.
Industry experts says young British drinkers, unlike their counterparts in Europe, Latin America, Southeast Asia and the former Soviet Union, do not consider whisky drinking to be fashionable.
They say young Britons associate whisky with old men in arm chairs, sitting in front of roaring fires rather than young people having fun in bars and nightclubs.
According to industry figures, the British consume 25 million fewer bottles of Scotch whisky a year then they did ten years ago.

Campbell Evans of the Scotch Whisky Association said "The UK accounts for only 10 per cent of the market, 90 per cent of it goes overseas. But Scotch is not on the rocks. It still accounts for more spirit sales in the UK than gin and vodka put together."

To change consumer perceptions, whisky companies are offering new products such as Loch Du and Red Devil and are also selling whisky with mixers. Many young drinkers in countries outside Britain drink whisky with cola, lemonade or ginger ale.
United Distiller's solution is to sell its Bell's whisky brand ready mixed with Irn Bru -- a fruit flavoured soft drink which is bright orange in colour and is popular in its homeland, Scotland.
The Bell's and Irn Bru combination is intended to encourage younger drinkers who may not like the strong taste of straight whisky to try the spirit in a different form.

While traditionalists believe that whisky should be drunk neat or with a little water, Evans said. "We have no problems with people mixing whisky with other things. New flavours and recent TV advertising gets people talking about whisky and that can only be a good thing."
Last year United Distillers and other spirits companies broke the self-imposed industry ban on advertising spirits on TV.

Ads for whisky brands including Bell's and Teacher's made by Allied Domecq Plc, the drinks and retail group, were broadcast in the run up to Christmas. These attempted to get away from traditional whisky imagery such as heather and tartan. Bell's ad featured young men having fun drinking whisky together in a bar.
This Christmas Allied Domecq will spend 4.0 million stg ($6.7 million) on advertising its spirits brands on TV.
